vo: Say a seller's factory calls their kids' toy certified.
Covered kids' products need a CPC, general-use ones a GCC.
Most wall-powered kids' toys have their own rule, part fifteen-oh-five.
The package needs ratings, required warnings, and a date or code.
Comment M and Z, we'll DM you the free CPSC finder.
caption:
Your factory says the wall-powered toy is certified. Certified to which rule?
Who it's made for decides the paperwork: children's products get a CPC, general-use products a GCC, when a CPSC rule applies.
Most toys for kids that run on 120-volt wall power fall under their own CPSC rule, 16 CFR part 1505 (video games are excluded).
That rule also sets what goes on the package: electrical ratings, required warnings, and the month and year it was made (or a date code).
Not sure which rules apply? Comment M&Z and we'll DM you the free CPSC Finder.

sources.claim: A finished product certificate is required when a CPSC rule, ban, standard or regulation applies
sources.quote: Finished products subject to a consumer product safety rule under the CPSA, or similar rule, ban, standard, or regulation under any other law enforced by the Commission, which are imported for consumption or warehousing, or are distributed in commerce, must be accompanied by a finished product certificate.

sources.claim: Two certificate types: CPC (children's) and GCC (general use)
sources.quote: There are two types of finished product certificates: Children's Product Certificates (CPCs) and General Certificates of Conformity (GCCs).

sources.claim: CPC is issued under CPSA 14(a)(2) (children's products); GCC under 14(a)(1)
sources.quote: Children's Product Certificate (CPC) means a certificate of compliance for a finished product issued pursuant to section 14(a)(2) of the CPSA, 15 U.S.C. 2063, and part 1107 of this chapter. ... General Certificate of Conformity (GCC) means a certificate of compliance for a finished product issued pursuant to section 14(a)(1) of the CPSA, 15 U.S.C. 2063(a)(1).

sources.claim: Part 1505 covers kids' toys powered from 120 V branch circuits; excludes <=30 V components, adult articles used incidentally by children, video games
sources.quote: any toy, game, or other article designed, labeled, advertised, or otherwise intended for use by children which is intended to be powered by electrical current from nominal 120 volt (110-125 v.) branch circuits. ... This definition does not include components which are powered by circuits of 30 volts r.m.s. (42.4 volts peak) or less, articles designed primarily for use by adults which may be used incidentally by children, or video games.

sources.claim: Part 1505 sets the requirements under which such toys are not banned
sources.quote: This part sets forth the requirements whereby electrically operated toys and other electrically operated articles intended for use by children (as defined in § 1505.1(a)(1)) are not banned toys or banned articles under § 1500.18(b)(1) of this chapter.

sources.claim: Package must show date (month/year or codes), electrical ratings, required precautionary statements
sources.quote: The shelf pack or package of the toy shall be labeled in accordance with the provisions of paragraph (d) of this section to indicate: (i) The date (month and year) of manufacture (or appropriate codes). (ii) The electrical ratings required by paragraph (c) of this section. (iii) Any precautionary statements required by paragraph (e) of this section.
